# The positional arguments list in the help page leaves out arguments that have no description

## What happens now

When a command takes several positional arguments and only one of them has a description, the help page shows only that one argument under "Positional arguments". The other positional arguments are missing from the list, even though they still show up in the usage line at the top of the help page. So the list and the usage line do not match, and a person reading the help cannot see every positional argument the command takes in one place.

## What should happen

As soon as one positional argument has a description, the "Positional arguments" list should show every positional argument the command takes. The ones without a description should still appear, with a blank description next to them. If none of the positional arguments has a description, the list should stay hidden, just as it does today.

## About this project

This project is a toolkit for building command line programs in Python. It lets a programmer describe the options and arguments a command takes, and it then builds the built-in help text, parses what the person typed, and reports errors. People who use those programs see this help text every time they run the program with the help flag.

## Problem this solves

A person reading the help page cannot see all the positional arguments a command accepts, so they have to guess the missing ones from the usage line. That makes the help text feel incomplete and forces people to look elsewhere for what the command needs.

## What changed

The "Positional arguments" list now matches the usage line. Once any one positional argument has a description, all of them are listed, and the ones without a description show a blank space next to them. When no positional argument has a description, no list appears, the same as before.

## Impact

Ease of use and a correct, complete help page.

## User experience

Before: a command takes three positional arguments and only the middle one has a description. The help page lists one argument, and the person using the program wonders what the other two are for.

After: the same command's help page lists all three positional arguments, with the two undescribed ones shown as blank, so the list lines up with the usage line above it.

- /workspace/docs/arguments.md
- /workspace/docs/documentation.md
- /workspace/tests/test_arguments.py

   3 │ # Arguments
   4 │ 
   5 │ ```{currentmodule} click
   6 │ ```
   7 │ 
   8 │ Arguments are:
   9 │ 
  10 │ * Are positional in nature.
  11 │ * Similar to a limited version of {ref}`options <options>` that
  12 │   can take an arbitrary number of inputs
  13 │ * Can take an optional `help` string shown in the `Positional arguments`
  14 │   section of the help page, or be {ref}`documented in the command docstring
  15 │   <documenting-arguments>`.
  16 │ 
  17 │ Useful and often used kwargs are:
  18 │ 
  19 │ * `help`: Help text for the argument.
  20 │ * `default`: Passes a default.
  21 │ * `nargs`: Sets the number of arguments. Set to -1 to take an arbitrary number.
  22 │ 
  23 │ ## Basic Arguments
  24 │ 
  25 │ A minimal {class}`click.Argument` solely takes one string argument:
  26 │ the name of the argument. This will assume the argument is required,
  27 │ has no default, and is of the type `str`.
  28 │ 
  29 │ Example:
  30 │ 
  31 │ ```{eval-rst}
  32 │ .. click:example::
  33 │ 
  34 │     @click.command()
  35 │     @click.argument('filename')
  36 │     def touch(filename: str):
  37 │         """Print FILENAME."""
  38 │         click.echo(filename)
  39 │ 
  40 │ And from the command line:
  41 │ 
  42 │ .. click:run::
  43 │ 
  44 │     invoke(touch, args=['foo.txt'])
  45 │ ```
  46 │ 
  47 │ An argument may be assigned a {ref}`parameter type <parameter-types>`.
  48 │ If no type is provided, the type of the default value is used if it is
  49 │ recognized, otherwise {data}`STRING` is used. If no default value is
  50 │ provided, the type is assumed to be {data}`STRING`. See
  51 │ {ref}`type-inference` for the types that are recognized.
  52 │ 
  53 │ ```{admonition} Note on Required Arguments
  54 │ :class: note
  55 │ 
  56 │    It is possible to make an argument required by setting
  57 │    `required=True`. It is not recommended since we think command line
  58 │    tools should gracefully degrade into becoming no ops. We think this
  59 │    because command line tools are often invoked with wildcard inputs
  60 │    and they should not error out if the wildcard is empty.
  61 │ ```
  62 │ 
  63 │ ## Multiple Arguments
  64 │ 
  65 │ To set the number of argument use the `nargs` kwarg. It can be set to
  66 │ any positive integer and -1. Setting it to -1, makes the number of
  67 │ arguments arbitrary (which is called variadic) and can only be used
  68 │ once. The arguments are then packed as a tuple and passed to the
  69 │ function.
  70 │ 
  71 │ ```{eval-rst}
  72 │ .. click:example::
  73 │ 
  74 │     @click.command()
  75 │     @click.argument('src', nargs=1)
  76 │     @click.argument('dsts', nargs=-1)
  77 │     def copy(src: str, dsts: tuple[str, ...]):
  78 │         """Move file SRC to DST."""
  79 │         for destination in dsts:
  80 │             click.echo(f"Copy {src} to folder {destination}")
  81 │ 
  82 │ And from the command line:
  83 │ 
  84 │ .. click:run::
  85 │ 
  86 │     invoke(copy, args=['foo.txt', 'usr/david/foo.txt', 'usr/mitsuko/foo.txt'])
  87 │ ```
  88 │ 
  89 │ ```{admonition} Note on Handling Files
  90 │ :class: note
  91 │ 
  92 │    This is not how you should handle files and files paths. This
  93 │    merely used as a simple example. See {ref}`handling-files` to learn
  94 │    more about how to handle files in parameters.
  95 │ ```
  96 │ 
  97 │ ## Argument Escape Sequences
  98 │ 
  99 │ If you want to process arguments that look like options, like a file
 100 │ named `-foo.txt` or `--foo.txt`, you must pass the `--` separator
 101 │ first. After you pass the `--`, you may only pass arguments. This is a
 102 │ common feature for POSIX command line tools.
 103 │ 
 104 │ Example usage:
 105 │ 
 106 │ ```{eval-rst}
 107 │ .. click:example::
 108 │ 
 109 │     @click.command()
 110 │     @click.argument('files', nargs=-1, type=click.Path())
 111 │     def touch(files):
 112 │         """Print all FILES file names."""
 113 │         for filename in files:
 114 │             click.echo(filename)
 115 │ 
 116 │ And from the command line:
 117 │ 
 118 │ .. click:run::

def format_arguments(self, ctx: Context, formatter: HelpFormatter) -> None:
        """Writes the arguments into the formatter.

        The section is only shown if at least one argument has a help
        record. Once it is shown, every argument is listed, even those
        without help text, so the list matches the usage line. Arguments
        without help text get a blank description.
        """
        args: list[tuple[str, str]] = []
        has_help = False

        for param in self.get_params(ctx):
            if not isinstance(param, Argument):
                continue

            rv = param.get_help_record(ctx)

            if rv is not None:
                has_help = True
                args.append(rv)
            else:
                args.append((param.make_metavar(ctx), ""))

        if has_help:
            with formatter.section(_("Positional arguments")):
                formatter.write_dl(args)
